title: Life-threatening asthma in a child
stem: Paediatric resus. A 5-year-old boy (about 18 kg) with known asthma has been wheezy for two days and much worse tonight. He is sitting forward, too breathless to talk, and becoming quiet. HR 170, RR 44, SpO2 88% in air. His father is with him.

phases.title: Recognise
phases.goal: Monitoring, oxygen, his weight; how severe is this?

phases.title: Nebulisers
phases.goal: From the drug cart, now: oxygen-driven nebulisers at the right doses.

phases.title: Help and his father
phases.goal: Call PICU and the anaesthetist; a quick history; answer his father honestly.

phases.title: IV treatment
phases.goal: Access and a gas, then an IV steroid and magnesium.

phases.title: Escalate
phases.goal: Not responding: IV salbutamol; the plan if he tires.

events.say: His chest has gone quiet. SpO2 82% and he is drowsy.
events.untreated: His chest went silent and nebulisers were never started.

events.say: Still very tight after the magnesium: SpO2 91%, tiring.

review.text: Ipratropium dose. Your notes give 125 microgram under 5 years. BTS gives 250 microgram for children 2–12 years, every 20–30 minutes for the first 2 hours.
Subcutaneous adrenaline. Your notes include it. It is not part of BTS acute asthma management; keep adrenaline for anaphylaxis.
Magnesium. BTS: 40 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 minutes; AHA PALS: 25–50 mg/kg over 15–30 minutes. The script's 40 mg/kg fits both.

notes:
Checked against BTS/SIGN British guideline on the management of asthma (2019; acute section retained in the 2024 BTS/NICE/SIGN update), RCUK paediatric life support and APLS.

Life-threatening features (children): SpO2 under 92%, silent chest, poor respiratory effort, altered consciousness, agitation, exhaustion, cyanosis, hypotension; PEF under 33% if measurable.

Treatment: high-flow oxygen to SpO2 94–98%; nebulised salbutamol (2.5 mg under 5 years, 5 mg 5 years and over) driven by oxygen, back-to-back; nebulised ipratropium 250 microgram every 20–30 minutes for the first 2 hours; steroids (oral prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg, max 40 mg, or IV hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg); IV magnesium sulfate 40 mg/kg (max 2 g) over 20 minutes; IV salbutamol 15 microgram/kg over 10 minutes if not responding; then PICU (aminophylline, infusions, ventilation). Your notes' doses match this, except: ipratropium 125 microgram under 5 years (BTS uses 250 microgram for 2–12 years), and subcutaneous adrenaline, which is not part of BTS acute asthma management (keep adrenaline for anaphylaxis).

Intubation is hazardous: experienced operator, ketamine, then low rate, long expiratory time, permissive hypercapnia (your ventilation notes are correct).

No routine chest X-ray unless pneumothorax, consolidation or life-threatening features not responding; no routine antibiotics.

Perfect script checked against a BTS/SIGN checklist, an AHA PALS respiratory checklist, an HKCEM-style scheme and a keyword scheme. Removed every wrong option (wrong nebuliser and IV doses, sedation, an X-ray first, the reassuring answer to his father). Added: oxygen (the station had none), his weight aloud, life-threatening asthma named, early PICU and anaesthetist, a history from his father in Cantonese, the gas read, and the plan if he tires including ventilation. The silent-chest event now waits 60 s after monitoring (was 45 s), long enough for the assessment.

wrong: 5 mg over 10 minutes, for any age

wrong: High rate to blow off the CO2 quickly

badge.name: Quiet Chest
badge.flavor: Silence is the danger sign. Back-to-back nebs, steroid, magnesium.

cards.q: Life-threatening asthma feature in a child?
cards.why: Also silent chest, poor effort, altered consciousness, cyanosis.

cards.q: Ipratropium dose in acute severe asthma (2–12 years)?
cards.why: Every 20–30 minutes in the first 2 hours.

cards.q: Oral prednisolone dose in paediatric acute asthma?
cards.why: Or IV hydrocortisone 4 mg/kg if unable to swallow.

cards.q: Routine chest X-ray in acute asthma?
options: No, only for complications or no response
Yes, in every child before treatment
Only in children over 5 years old
Before starting nebulisers, to exclude a foreign body

cards.q: Why use oxygen to drive nebulisers in acute asthma?
options: Salbutamol can worsen V/Q mismatch and hypoxia
Medical air is unavailable in most EDs
Oxygen dilates the airways on its own

script.say: Monitoring on, please: ECG, blood pressure and SpO2. He's 5: (5 + 4) × 2, about 18 kg. High-flow oxygen, 15 litres via a non-rebreather, aiming for 94 to 98%.
He can't talk; accessory muscles, recession, tiring. The chest is very quiet on both sides: a silent chest. Drowsy, pale, dusky lips. SpO2 88%: this is life-threatening asthma.
Salbutamol 5 mg nebulised, oxygen-driven, back to back, with ipratropium 250 micrograms.
Please call my senior, PICU and the anaesthetist now: he's tiring with a silent chest. No sedation for him: it can stop his breathing.
What inhalers does he use, and has he ever been in intensive care for his asthma? Any allergies to medicines?
script.do: Blue and brown inhalers, not always used; PICU last year; no allergies.

script.say: When a chest goes quiet it can mean very little air is moving. He needs strong treatment now. Stay by him and keep him calm.
IV access, and a blood gas: a normal or rising CO2 means he's tiring. A chest X-ray only if he doesn't respond or I suspect a pneumothorax.
Hydrocortisone 4 mg per kg, 72 mg IV. Magnesium sulfate 40 mg per kg, 720 mg IV over 20 minutes.
Still very tight after the magnesium: IV salbutamol 15 micrograms per kg, 270 micrograms over 10 minutes.

Then a salbutamol infusion, and aminophylline in PICU. If he needs intubating: the most experienced person, with ketamine; then a low rate and a long expiratory time, accepting a high CO2: permissive hypercapnia.
